Turuvekere • Turuvekere Taluk • Tumakuru District • Karnataka

Inscriptional settlement history: 1263 and 1267 CE
Gangadhareshwara Temple: proposed 16th–17th-century architectural attribution

Nandi: proposed Post Vijayanagara attribution
At Gangadhareshwara, the name of the deity becomes a sculptural composition.

Gangadevi sits in padmasana above the linga, her hands displaying abhaya and varada. 

A brilliantly polished Nandi establishes the sacred axis towards the shrine. East of the temple, a large bell carved from soapstone produces a metallic resonance when gently sounded.

These features belong to the temple’s later architectural and sculptural history.

The inscriptions of Turuvekere preserve an earlier phase: the creation and administration of a Hoysala agrahara during the reign of Narasimha III.

𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗨𝗩𝗘𝗬𝗔𝗞𝗘𝗥𝗘 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗜𝗡𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗣𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗔𝗟 𝗦𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗟𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧

Epigraphia Carnatica, Vol. XII classifies the Turuvekere records under the historical Tiptur Taluk as Tp 2–4. The town presently lies in Turuvekere Taluk.

Rice’s transcription preserves the place name as:

𝗧𝘂𝗿𝘂𝘃𝗲𝘆𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗲

In 1263 CE, during the reign of Hoysala Narasimha III, Sovanna-dannayaka received Turuveyakere and organised it as an agrahara divided into ninety-five shares.

The settlement received the formal name:

𝗦𝗮𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗷𝗻𝗮-𝗦𝗿𝗶-𝗩𝗶𝗷𝗮𝘆𝗮-𝗡𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗵𝗮𝗽𝘂𝗿𝗮

The record describes the mahajanas regulating dry fields, rice fields, tanks, ponds, taxes and customary dues. Cultivation, irrigation and collective obligations were therefore embedded within the administration of the agrahara.

A second record of 1263 CE describes the mahajanas assembling as a maha-sabhe inside the Prasanna-Chenna-Kesava Temple.

They consolidated two shares associated with Aradhya Kotisankara and issued their decision as a stone charter.

The temple functioned here as a place of worship and as the documented meeting space of the settlement assembly.

A third record, dated 1267 CE, records a grant to Sovanna-dannayaka of a house site near the northern gateway of the deity’s street and land for a garden.

It also preserves a land transaction involving Govinda-bhatta, conducted in Sovanna’s presence with the approval of the temple priests.

The inscriptional name Prasanna-Chenna-Kesava and the present name Chennigaraya are recorded separately. Later scholarship discusses these records in relation to the present Chennigaraya Temple.

The inscriptions securely date Turuvekere’s agrahara, assembly and land administration. The surviving Gangadhareshwara Temple belongs to a separately studied architectural phase.

𝗔 𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗜𝗩𝗔 𝗣𝗛𝗔𝗦𝗘

Reshma Anjum’s study proposes a broad 16th–17th-century attribution for the present north-facing Gangadhareshwara Temple.

She describes a plan comprising the garbhagriha, sukhanasi, navaranga, mukhamantapa and a frontal pillared hall.

Her study identifies the worshipping couple represented upon the deepastambha as the Hagalavadi palegara Anne Nayaka and his wife, associating the temple’s construction with his period.

This identification is best treated as a scholarly proposal. Further epigraphic and architectural documentation can clarify the patronage and construction sequence.

Rice’s 1897 Gazetteer supplies the wider political setting.

It records that the Hagalavadi chief Sali Nayak brought Turuvekere within his territory and entrusted its government to Chikka Nayak and Anne Nayak. The brothers are credited with constructing the outer fort, enlarging the tank and undertaking further improvements in the town.

Turuvekere entered the Mysore kingdom under Chikka Deva Raja in 1676.

The temple can therefore be read within a sacred landscape that continued to receive patronage, sculpture and architectural additions long after the foundation of the Hoysala agrahara.

𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 — 𝗚𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔 𝗔𝗕𝗢𝗩𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗔

ಗಂಗಾಧರೇಶ್ವರ
Gangadhareshwara — Shiva who bears Ganga

Anjum describes the linga and its serpent-hooded composition as carved from a single stone.

Above the linga, Gangadevi sits in padmasana, her hands displaying abhaya and varada.
Begin your observation from behind Nandi.

Follow the central axis into the sanctum and then raise your gaze above the linga. The image gives visible form to the temple’s name: Shiva, Ganga and the linga are brought together within one sacred composition.

The sculpture translates the idea of Gangadhara directly into the visual and ritual centre of the temple.

𝗡𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗜 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗢𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗦𝗖𝗔𝗣𝗘

Rice described the large recumbent Nandi in 1897 as elaborately carved from black hornblende obtained from Karekal-gudda and retaining a brilliant polish.

The Gazetteer places the old Karekal-gudda quarry about half a mile east of Kadahalli.

This connect the sacred image with Turuvekere’s surrounding geological and craft landscape.

Look closely at the transition from mass to ornament.

The broad back and folded limbs carry necklaces, bells, harness bands and carefully finished surface planes. Light moves continuously across the polished stone, strengthening Nandi’s physical presence before the shrine.

The sculpture records more than devotional iconography. It also reflects the identification, selection, transport, carving and polishing of stone from the region surrounding Turuvekere.

𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗦 𝗦𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗗

East of the temple stands a large bell carved from soapstone.

Its profile follows the familiar form of a cast-metal temple bell, while its substance belongs to the sculptor’s stone workshop. When gently sounded, it produces a metallic resonance.

The sculptor therefore worked with form, thickness and the acoustic properties of stone.

The bell deserves documentation as both sculpture and acoustic heritage. A measured drawing, high-resolution 3D record and controlled sound recording can preserve its dimensions, surface treatment and resonance.

Temple-guided demonstrations can combine visitor understanding with careful handling.

𝗞𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗔 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗔𝗥 𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘𝗦

On the upper portion of a pillar, Bedara Kannappa appears at the culminating moment of his devotion.

Having offered one eye to Shiva, he places his foot upon the linga to mark the position of the second while preparing his next offering.

The sculptor communicates the narrative through the inclined body, lifted leg, arrow and direct physical relationship between the devotee and the linga.

Another pillar carries Ganesha.

The kalyana-mantapa carvings include Bhringi, Nandi and Vishnu playing musical instruments, together with a dancing form of Shiva.

These images reward a slower passage through the hall. The sacred narrative continues above eye level, across pillar faces and through the spaces connecting the sanctum, navaranga and outer mantapa.

𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗚𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗗𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗛𝗪𝗔𝗥𝗔 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗦

Turuvekere preserves several historical layers within one compact sacred landscape.

The inscriptions of 1263–1267 CE establish an agrahara, its maha-sabhe and its systems of land, water and revenue administration.

The present Gangadhareshwara Temple carries a proposed 16th–17th-century architectural attribution and a scholarly association with Anne Nayaka.

The polished Nandi carries a connection with the hornblende quarry landscape near Kadahalli.

The linga, Gangadevi, Kannappa pillar and resonant stone bell preserve a Shaiva experience shaped through image, surface, movement and sound.

A Kannada–English interpretation panel can present these phases separately and map Turuvekere’s Gangadhareshwara, Chennigaraya, Moole Shankareshwara and Beteraya temples.

It can also distinguish present and inscriptional names, explain the agrahara records and connect Nandi with the local quarry landscape.

Measured architectural drawings, inscription maps, high-resolution photography, 3D documentation and acoustic recording can strengthen scholarship, visitor understanding and community stewardship.

At Turuvekere, begin with the inscriptions and their record of collective administration.

Carry that history into the later temple landscape.

Then allow Gangadevi above the linga, the polished Nandi, the narrative pillars and the stone bell to guide the eye—and the ear—across centuries.

𝗦𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗖𝗘𝗦

• B. Lewis Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica, Vol. XII: Inscriptions in the Tumkur District, Mysore Government Central Press, 1904, Tiptur Taluk, Tp 2–4; Roman text, pp. 68–70; translations, pp. 42–43.

• B. Lewis Rice, Mysore: A Gazetteer Compiled for Government, revised edition, Vol. II: Mysore by Districts, Westminster: Archibald Constable and Company, 1897, pp. 186 and 205.

• Reshma Anjum, Temples of Tumkur District: A Historical Study, PhD thesis, Department of Studies and Research in History and Archaeology, Tumkur University, 2018, printed pp. 103–106; PDF pp. 113–116.

• Tumakuru District Administration, “Organisation,” for the present Turuvekere Taluk classification.

Lisp + LLM: A Better Way to Build Image Prompts

For OpenAI Build Week, I built an npm package called Spellcast Universe to improve the aesthetics and efficiency of image generation with Codex and GPT Image 2.

With just a single command:
spellcast "An apple" 4

You can generate four aesthetically refined apple illustrations at once with a single command, making Codex image generation up to 4× faster.

Spellcast Universe transforms a simple idea into a complete prompt pipeline, enabling Codex to generate four polished apple images in seconds. Instead of spending time manually crafting long prompts, creators can focus on the idea itself while the framework handles prompt composition and image generation.

So, how did Spellcast Universe come to life?

Since the launch of GPT Image 2, I have spent a great deal of time studying the model and experimenting with how it generates images. While working with anime-style imagery, I found that Image 2 often produced excessive visual noise. This became the starting point of my research into prompt engineering.

I began by structuring and modularizing prompts, and developed a technique I call the Noise Reduction Ladder. I then continued studying many different kinds of image-generation prompts in greater depth.

One of the most important things I learned is that prompts are not a universal language. A prompt that works for one model may not work the same way for another. For that reason, my research has been focused specifically on prompt engineering for OpenAI GPT Image 2.

I realized that the power of Lisp macros could turn one stable prompt into 100, 1,000, or even 10,000 controlled variations. Lisp can manage the boundaries and perform symbolic compilation, while Codex brings creativity into the structure. To me, this is the best combination: Lisp provides control and scalability, and Codex provides imagination.

That idea led me to create Prompt Universe.

Prompt Universe treats prompts as structured and evolvable programs rather than disposable blocks of text. A stable prompt becomes a reusable seed. Lisp macros can then expand that seed across different creative dimensions while preserving its important rules, structure, and visual identity.

After building the ability to evolve a single spell into a large family of prompts, only one major problem remained: generating all of the images quickly.

I spent a great deal of time studying Codex and its imagegen skill. I then built local scripts that allow Codex to control multiple Terminal windows and invoke additional Codex workers in parallel. The jobs are divided into controlled waves so that image generation can be accelerated without colliding with rate limits.

In other words, the system makes the fullest possible use of Codex's image-generation capacity within each available time window. It is highly efficient, but it is also practical for ordinary users who want to generate many creative variations without manually repeating the same workflow.

I called this tool image-gen-runner, and it is also being prepared for release.

The first challenge was understanding why anime-style generations from GPT Image 2 could become noisy or visually fragmented. Solving that problem required much more than adding negative keywords. I had to study prompt hierarchy, material descriptions, semantic conflicts, attention priority, and the relationship between structure and visual stability. That research eventually became the Noise Reduction Ladder and the broader philosophy behind Prompt Universe.

The second challenge was scale. Generating hundreds or thousands of useful prompt variations is only valuable if those prompts can also be turned into images efficiently. Building image-gen-runner required me to study how Codex handles image generation, how to coordinate multiple workers, how to divide jobs safely, and how to avoid wasting capacity or overwhelming rate limits.

The final challenge was bringing these two very different systems together. Prompt Universe focuses on creativity, symbolic structure, compilation, and controlled evolution. image-gen-runner focuses on orchestration, parallelism, and generation efficiency. They were originally separate tools with separate workflows.

Participating in OpenAI Build Week gave me an opportunity to rethink both projects.

Instead of keeping Prompt Universe and image-gen-runner as separate tools, I decided to integrate them into a single CLI. The result is Spellcast Universe: a tool that combines Codex creativity, Lisp-powered symbolic compilation, scalable prompt evolution, and parallel image generation in one workflow.

I believe this makes the original ideas more complete and much more useful. A user can begin with a creative idea, turn it into a structured spell, evolve it into many controlled prompts, and then automatically cast those prompts into images through Codex—all with both creativity and efficiency.

🚨 99% of Python beginners learn the wrong way.
They jump between random YouTube videos... Watch 100 tutorials... Build nothing.
If I had to start Python again in 2026, this is the exact roadmap I'd follow👇
🐍 Python Master Cheatsheet (2026)
1. Basics
Learn variables, indentation, comments, input/output, and Python syntax. This is the foundation—skip it and everything else feels confusing.
2. Data Types
Understand integers, floats, strings, booleans, lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries. Every Python program is built on these.
3. Operators
Master arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment operators to perform calculations and make decisions.
4. Control Flow
Use if, elif, else, for, and while loops to control how your program behaves.
5. Functions
Write reusable code with def, parameters, return values, default arguments, and clean function design.
6. Strings
Manipulate text using slicing, formatting, .split(), .join(), .replace(), and f-strings.
7. Lists
Store collections of data. Learn indexing, slicing, appending, removing, sorting, and looping.
8. Tuples
Immutable collections that are faster and safer when your data shouldn't change.
9. Sets
Remove duplicates, perform unions/intersections, and speed up lookups.
10. Dictionaries
Store data as key-value pairs. Essential for APIs, JSON, and real-world applications.
11. List Comprehensions
Write cleaner and more Pythonic code in a single line.
12. Lambda Functions
Create small anonymous functions for sorting, filtering, and quick operations.
13. File Handling
Read, write, and manage files using open(), with, and file modes.
14. Exception Handling
Use try, except, finally, and raise so your programs don't crash unexpectedly.
15. Modules
Leverage Python's standard library (math, os, datetime, random) instead of reinventing the wheel.
16. Built-in Functions
Master len(), sum(), range(), sorted(), max(), min() and dozens more to write efficient code.
17. Pip
Install and manage packages like NumPy, Pandas, Requests, and Flask with ease.
18. Virtual Environments
Keep project dependencies isolated to avoid version conflicts.
19. Magic (Dunder) Methods
Learn __init__, __str__, __repr__, and more to write professional object-oriented Python.
20. Best Practices
Write readable code, follow PEP 8, use meaningful names, handle errors, and build projects consistently.
📌 Master these 20 topics, and you'll have a strong Python foundation for: • AI & Machine Learning • Data Science • Automation • Web Development • Backend APIs • Cybersecurity

VA LIVE is now live on-chain! 🎉💃💃

One thing about me is that I’m always curious about how technology can make work simpler and more efficient.

As an Admin Virtual Assistant who’s also exploring Web3 and AI, I spend a lot of time thinking about systems, productivity, and the repetitive tasks that slow founders and small teams down.

That curiosity led to VA LIVE , built to participate in  the OKX Genesis Hackathon.

VA LIVE is an AI-powered on-chain agent designed to support administrative workflows. It’s not built to replace the value that great Virtual Assistants bring, it’s built to automate repetitive tasks so people can spend more time on work that actually needs human thinking and creativity.

Here are a few things VA Live can help with:

• Turn messy notes into clear SOPs your team can actually follow.

• Organize your inbox by summarizing emails, prioritizing them, and even drafting replies.

• Create research briefs that compare tools or vendors and recommend the best option.

• Build your personal brand with a polished bio, content pillars, and ready-to-use post ideas.

• Set up a new business with SOPs, email templates, and an organized operations structure.

Services start from 0.08 USDT, so anyone can try them out.
